title: The animal inside coffee’s most unforgettable story
dek: Kopi luwak turned an unlikely production method into a global talking point. Its next chapter should begin with evidence about the beans—and the animals.
heroAlt: Illustrative coffee cherries and botanical detail accompanying a report on civet coffee.
heroCaption: Editorial botanical illustration. It depicts coffee plants, not a documented kopi luwak farm.
standfirst: Few coffee stories travel as easily as this one: an animal eats the fruit, people recover the seeds, and the resulting cup becomes a luxury. The story is memorable. Whether the coffee deserves its price is a different question, and whether the animal lived well is another. Research reviewed through 13 October 2026 makes those distinctions essential.

sections.title: A story that almost tells itself
paragraphs: Kopi luwak is coffee made from seeds recovered after coffee cherries pass through civets. Despite the familiar expression “cat coffee,” the animals are civets, not domestic cats. The name describes a treatment of coffee, not a separate botanical species. That distinction matters: an unusual processing story cannot explain everything about the plant, the harvest or the eventual drink. A scientific review published in December 2024 treats the product as a combination of chemistry, authentication, market behaviour and ethics. Read the scientific review.

The narrative has the economy of a folk tale: a surprising animal, a hidden transformation and an expensive object. Coffeedant’s reading is that this structure helps explain why people remember it. That is an editorial interpretation, not a measured claim about an entire generation’s awareness. It is also an invitation to notice what disappears from a memorable story. A buyer can repeat the origin in one sentence while knowing almost nothing about the producer, the animal’s conditions or the lot in the bag.

sections.title: Two questions that a luxury label cannot answer
paragraphs: Start with two independent questions. First, did these particular beans pass through a civet? Second, how was that civet treated? Evidence answering the first does not automatically answer the second. The 2024 review describes laboratory approaches to authenticity, including spectroscopy, electronic noses, chromatography and statistical analysis of chemical profiles. Such methods concern product identity. They are not certificates of animal welfare, nor does a successful laboratory distinction establish that a coffee will taste better than another.

This separation changes the conversation with a seller. Rather than asking whether the product is “real,” ask what the word means in that transaction. Does the answer identify a farm or collection area? Can a dated lot be followed through collection, processing and sale? Is a laboratory result linked to that lot, or is it an attractive document about another sample? These are questions about the strength and relevance of evidence, not accusations. A story becomes more informative when its supporting records refer to the coffee actually being sold.

sections.title: The animal cannot be edited out
paragraphs: A peer-reviewed investigation assessed 29 civet-coffee tourism plantations in Bali and eight wildlife markets. Researchers recorded 99 civets at plantations and 136 in markets. Diet, hygiene, water availability and mobility influenced body condition. None of the observed civets met all five freedoms used in the assessment. That is a serious finding about the sampled facilities; it is not a census of every kopi luwak producer. The sample and its limits should travel together whenever the result is quoted. See the welfare study.

For a reader, the implication is practical. A polished visitor experience and an animal visible beside a coffee counter cannot substitute for independently inspectable management information. A welfare discussion needs to be about the living animal, rather than the photographic appeal of its role in production. Coffeedant’s editorial recommendation is to ask whether the seller can explain care, diet, housing, sourcing and independent oversight in concrete terms. If the response stays with rarity and price, the central question has not been answered.

sections.title: What the 2025–2026 research adds—and does not
paragraphs: A 2025 study presents a more optimistic view of potential sustainability practices among participating legal producers. Its method includes one focus group and 12 interviews. That can illuminate how participants describe their operations and the choices they believe matter. It cannot establish the conditions of an entire industry, and it does not cancel findings from direct welfare observations. Different studies may examine different businesses and different kinds of evidence. Read the 2025 qualitative study.

In 2026, a laboratory study compared fresh and dried Typica civet-coffee samples from seven animals. The researchers found changes in microbial and metabolite profiles during drying. Crucially, they did not conduct sensory evaluation. A chemical difference is therefore not a demonstrated advantage in the cup. This is an instructive example of how scientific novelty can become overstated in marketing: “different” is a description; “better” requires a defined comparison and evidence suited to that claim. Read the 2026 laboratory study.

sections.title: Rarity is a reason to look closer
paragraphs: An unusual route to a bean can justify curiosity without settling its sensory value. When reading a premium label, separate the claims into identity, production method, welfare, scarcity and taste. They ask for different evidence. A laboratory authentication result might support identity. A lot record might support provenance. Independent observation might support an account of animal management. A blind comparison could inform a personal judgement of taste. None is interchangeable with the others, and a high price does not do the work of all four.

A useful thought experiment is to hide the production story while comparing coffees. If the story were revealed only afterwards, what would you want to know about your first impression? This is a suggested tasting exercise, not a report of a Coffeedant experiment. Its point is to make room for both sensory pleasure and informed choice. A drink can be fascinating because of its story. The reader still deserves to understand how much of the attraction comes from the cup and how much comes from the narrative around it.

sections.title: The next chapter needs a chain of evidence
paragraphs: For consumers, the strongest next step is not another superlative. It is a clearer chain from sourcing to the finished lot. Ask for the production location, collection method, dates, animal-management explanation and any independent assessment. Ask what the retailer has actually verified. The answers may be incomplete; incompleteness should remain visible rather than being filled with assumptions. A claim of wild collection is a claim to investigate, not an automatic shortcut to certainty.

This is why kopi luwak belongs in an editorial conversation about modern coffee. It exposes the power of origin stories and the limits of novelty as a quality signal. The responsible question is not whether the tale is entertaining—it plainly has an arresting structure—but whether the information behind it is as compelling as the tale itself. For Coffeedant, a luxury worth understanding should disclose its evidence with the same care it gives its packaging. Curiosity becomes knowledge when the animal and the actual lot stay in the frame.

faqs.q: Is kopi luwak made by cats?
faqs.a: It involves civets, not domestic cats. “Cat coffee” is a memorable but misleading shorthand.

faqs.q: Does civet processing prove that the coffee tastes better?
faqs.a: No. A processing difference is not a universal sensory ranking. The 2026 drying study discussed here did not include tasting.

faqs.q: Can a chemical test prove humane production?
faqs.a: No. Product authentication and animal welfare require different kinds of evidence.

title: Robusta’s second act has a water problem
dek: A neglected species is gaining attention, breeding investment and export volume. The exciting story becomes more useful when we stop calling it climate-proof.
heroAlt: Illustrative coffee cherries and leaves introducing an article about Coffea canephora.
heroCaption: Editorial botanical illustration. Species and growing conditions should be verified from producer records.
standfirst: The coffee conversation is making more room for Coffea canephora, commonly called robusta. That shift deserves curiosity. It also deserves precision: new breeding candidates are not finished varieties, rising exports are not a specialty-market census, and warmth tolerance is not a guarantee against drought. A major August 2026 scientific review brings water back into the picture.

sections.title: Meet the plant before judging the cup
paragraphs: World Coffee Research describes Coffea canephora as originating in central and western sub-Saharan Africa. Its wild populations occur mainly in humid evergreen forest understory, across elevations of approximately 50 to 1,500 metres. This is a better starting point than treating robusta as a flavour stereotype. It is a plant with a geography and a range of growing environments. A species name gives a reader useful information, but it is not a complete description of an individual lot. Explore the WCR botanical catalog.

When approaching an unfamiliar coffee, ask which details are being offered and which are being left to your imagination. A named producer, harvest, processing method and roast provide a more informative introduction than a single word on a bag. Coffeedant’s recommendation is to make the question smaller: not “Do I like robusta?” but “What can I learn from this identifiable coffee?” That formulation makes room for preference without turning one encounter into a verdict on a whole species.

sections.title: The numbers show movement, not the whole story
paragraphs: In November 2024, World Coffee Research placed robusta’s share of global production at about 40%, compared with 25% in the early 1990s. Those are dated figures, not a live October 2026 estimate. They nevertheless describe a substantial change in the production mix over time. The organization’s research agenda includes quality for different markets, from commercial through specialty. The story is broader than a sudden fashionable rediscovery. Read The roots of Robusta.

The ICO’s current summary adds a recent trade signal. In the twelve months ending August 2026, robusta exports reached 61.05 million 60-kilogram bags, against 54.48 million in the comparison period. Arabica exports were 81.39 million, against 85.97 million. These numbers measure export volume, not fine-robusta demand or consumer approval. Calling them proof that specialty robusta has conquered the market would answer a question the data did not ask. Read the ICO market summary.

That distinction is the foundation of a useful trend report. One can observe more trade and more research attention while leaving the size of a specific premium segment unresolved. The uncertainty does not weaken the story; it tells the reader where the next meaningful evidence should come from.

sections.title: A thousand candidates are a beginning
paragraphs: World Coffee Research’s July 2025 update reported progress with controlled crosses and clonal propagation after breeding work began in 2024. A September 2026 update describes 1,000 clones selected as a founding population and being multiplied for national partners. The precise word is candidates: this is a breeding population, not an announcement of 1,000 proven new commercial varieties. Read the July 2025 update; read the 2026 clone update.

For an editorial reader, the interesting change is the seriousness of the question being asked. Which combinations of traits should future planting material pursue, and how should farmers’ needs shape the work? A promising candidate can be worth studying without being ready to recommend everywhere. When a brand cites a breeding project, ask whether it is describing a research objective, an experimental result or a variety already evaluated for the stated conditions.

These stages should stay distinct in visual explanations too. A seedling image beside the phrase “future of coffee” is evocative, but a clear caption should tell us what stage we are seeing. Coffeedant’s interpretation is that sustained breeding attention is a stronger signal than a fashionable claim of instant transformation.

sections.title: The 2026 challenge to an easy climate story
paragraphs: A review published on 27 August 2026 in Sustainable Development challenges broad claims of climate resilience for farmed robusta. It emphasizes soil and terrestrial water availability, irrigation, shade and farming inputs. The authors argue that some climate analyses overlook water relationships and the extent to which cultivation depends on irrigation. This is a substantive critique to attribute to its authors, not a reason to declare every farm or climate model equivalent. Read The Sustainability of Robusta Coffee Under Global Change.

The distinction it brings into focus is simple: enduring warm conditions and delivering dependable harvests when water is limited are different propositions. Coffeedant would therefore avoid “climate-proof” altogether. Such a label compresses a landscape into a promise. The reader needs to know what stress is being discussed, under which management conditions, and what evidence supports the claim.

A more informative illustration places rainfall, soil water, irrigation and shade beside temperature. The point is not to invent a universal formula for farmers. It is to prevent a single thermometer from representing every condition a crop faces. The most credible climate story leaves room for local questions rather than making a global guarantee from a species name.

sections.title: Give quality a more precise vocabulary
paragraphs: Species, processing and roast should be separate entries in a coffee description. If a label blends them into one identity, it becomes difficult to know what a comparison means. A heavily roasted blended coffee and a differently handled single lot are not a tidy species experiment. This is a principle for interpreting comparisons, not a claim that one treatment is intrinsically superior. Useful editorial tasting begins by naming the question and the variables that remain different.

At home, an approachable exercise is to compare two identifiable coffees while recording the recipes and your own preferences. Keep expectations visible. Write down what you thought the name would mean, then describe what you actually noticed without forcing the notes to match the label. This is a suggested reader activity; Coffeedant has not conducted a tasting for this article.

The resulting judgement can be modest and still valuable: “I preferred this lot in this preparation” is more informative than “this species is good” or “this species is bad.” It also gives a retailer something practical to respond to when recommending the next coffee.

sections.title: The next signals worth watching
paragraphs: For the next chapter, watch for named varieties evaluated in named environments, rather than broad announcements that coffee has been saved. Watch for a transparent distinction between export growth and premium-market development. In descriptions of individual lots, watch for producer, harvest and handling information that survives beyond an attractive origin paragraph. These are editorial criteria for reading new claims; they are not a forecast of which origin or business will succeed.

The same curiosity should extend to resources. If a climate claim depends on irrigation or another management practice, that dependence belongs in the story. Omitting it makes the system appear simpler than the evidence suggests. A sophisticated coffee culture can celebrate a plant’s possibilities while asking what makes those possibilities practical.

Robusta’s second act is compelling precisely because it is unfinished. There is a substantial crop, a changing trade picture, new breeding work and an active scientific debate about resilience. The reader does not need a heroic species to stay interested. A clearer account of the plant, the people evaluating it and the conditions they must contend with offers something better: a trend that can be followed intelligently as the evidence develops.

title: Decaf deserves a place at the tasting table
dek: The more interesting decaf story is about identity, choice and a clearer explanation of processing—not miracle growth rates or solvent scares.
heroAlt: Illustrative coffee preparation scene accompanying an explanation of decaffeination.
heroCaption: Editorial illustration. The cup is a visual introduction, not a laboratory measurement of caffeine.
standfirst: A serious coffee menu can treat decaf as a coffee with an origin and a processing history. That is Coffeedant’s editorial proposition, not a claim that every decaf tastes exceptional. To understand the current conversation, follow how caffeine is removed, what the labels actually say, and where the evidence stops. Research checked through 13 October 2026.

sections.title: Begin with the coffee, then ask about the caffeine
paragraphs: Imagine a menu that gives its decaf the same descriptive space as its other coffees: producer or origin, handling, roast and the method used to remove caffeine. This is a design proposal for better information, not a report of a universal industry shift. It changes the reader’s starting question from “Why would anyone choose this?” to “What is this coffee, and how was it made?” The choice becomes easier to understand when the product has an identity.

That approach also keeps preference personal. Someone can be interested in the ritual, the flavour or the freedom to choose a different caffeine level without needing a story that makes decaf virtuous. Coffeedant’s reading of the current moment is that the category deserves a more demanding vocabulary. It should be possible to discuss an ordinary decaf honestly, an excellent one enthusiastically and an unclear label critically—using the same care that applies to other coffees.

sections.title: Read the renaissance without inflating the numbers
paragraphs: Swiss Water’s annual results, released on 12 March 2026, offer a useful reality check. The company reported 2025 processed volume up 2% and revenue up 49%, while fourth-quarter volume declined 2%. Those figures describe one decaffeination business. They do not measure the entire global decaf market, and a revenue increase is not equivalent to people drinking that much more coffee. Read the 2025 full-year results.

A thoughtful trend article should hold those distinctions in view. One company’s investment, marketing and results can reveal attention to a category without establishing its universal trajectory. “Renaissance” is an editorial frame for reconsidering the product; it should not be disguised as a percentage lifted from an opaque forecast. A claim about more sales, a claim about better taste and a claim about changing social attitudes would each need evidence of its own.

The useful next question is therefore what makes the product more legible to its buyer. Better descriptions, explicit processing information and identified lots can improve the conversation even before a market-wide growth rate is available.

sections.title: Four labels, four routes to the same question
paragraphs: An industry explanation from the Coffee Association of Canada describes decaffeination as moistening green coffee, applying an extracting agent and drying the beans afterwards. It lists water, carbon dioxide, ethyl acetate and methylene chloride among the agents used. These are ways to remove caffeine before roasting; they are not four new coffee species. Read the process overview.

Swiss Water’s own process explanation describes green coffee extract and carbon filtration. Caffeine moves from beans into the extract, and filters capture it. A useful original diagram follows that movement rather than decorating the word “water” with purity imagery. Coffeedant calls this water-based decaffeination. The company’s familiar “chemical-free” language is marketing shorthand, not literal chemistry. See the manufacturer’s process explanation.

Compressed carbon dioxide is another extracting medium. Technical research examines the relationship among caffeine, water and CO₂ under processing conditions. A label naming CO₂ tells you something about the extraction route; it does not by itself tell you how a particular coffee will taste. Likewise, the phrase “sugarcane decaf” should lead to a specific explanation of the ethyl-acetate process, not an assumption that the beans were simply sweetened. Read the CO₂ technical paper.

sections.title: Replace alarming names with useful context
paragraphs: The current US rule permits methylene chloride as a residue from decaffeination at no more than 10 parts per million in decaffeinated roasted coffee and instant-coffee extract. A separate US rule permits ethyl acetate as a decaffeination solvent under good manufacturing practice. These are specific US regulations, not a claim about every jurisdiction or every product. 21 CFR 173.255; 21 CFR 173.228.

Process literacy means being able to state those facts without converting a chemical name into a health verdict. A frightening association is not a measurement of exposure in the coffee being discussed. Equally, a reassuring adjective on a bag is not a complete account of the process. This article does not claim that a label can determine an individual health outcome; it explains how to read a production description without substituting slogans for evidence.

For a shopping decision, ask the seller to identify the method and the processor if available. If avoiding a particular method is your preference, a clear answer allows you to act on it. There is no need to turn that preference into a universal ranking of coffees or people who drink them.

sections.title: Decaf does not mean caffeine-free
paragraphs: The FDA says an eight-US-fluid-ounce cup of decaf coffee typically contains 2 to 15 milligrams of caffeine. That is a range, not a measurement of the cup beside you. Product and serving details matter. “Decaf” should therefore not be read as “zero,” and a larger serving should not be assumed to have the same total as the reference cup. Read the FDA explanation.

A useful graphic shows the reference serving and its range, with the caption doing as much work as the number. It should avoid a tiny precise-looking marker labelled “your coffee” when no test was performed. The underlying lesson applies beyond decaf: a category average or typical range is valuable information, but it does not become an individualized result merely because it is placed in an interactive calculator.

This distinction also changes the language of a menu. “Lower-caffeine choice” is more informative than implying complete absence. Where a reader needs a specific caffeine amount, the next step is to seek product-specific information rather than treating any decaf label as an analytical certificate.

sections.title: Give the cup a fair, specific comparison
paragraphs: To evaluate a decaf at home, begin with a question you can actually answer: do you enjoy this identifiable coffee in the preparation you use? Record the coffee, roast information, recipe and your own observations. If comparing two products, note the differences you cannot control. An origin change or a different roast means the exercise is not a clean test of decaffeination methods. This is a suggested reader exercise; Coffeedant has not conducted a blind tasting for this story.

Use the process label as one line of information rather than as the conclusion. A method can be explained beautifully while a specific product disappoints you. Conversely, finding a coffee you enjoy does not prove that its method must always win. The fairest judgement keeps the product, preparation and preference together.

That is the editorial case for decaf’s place at the tasting table. It deserves neither a diminished set of expectations nor automatic praise for existing. It deserves an identity, a clear explanation and a reader free to choose. The conversation becomes richer when removing a stimulant does not remove the questions we normally ask about coffee.

title: When coffee tastes like strawberry, what happened?
dek: Anaerobic, inoculated, co-fermented, infused: the exciting new vocabulary of coffee works best when the method is as clear as the flavour.
heroAlt: Illustrative coffee cherries introducing a report on fermentation and processing labels.
heroCaption: Editorial botanical illustration. The process diagram below is explanatory, not a depiction of a specific farm.
standfirst: A vivid fruit note can be an invitation to explore, but it is not a laboratory test of how a coffee was made. In January 2026, the Specialty Coffee Association published a substantial report about coffee with added ingredients and the language around it. The emerging frontier is not simply stronger flavour. It is a more transparent account of how that flavour was pursued.

sections.title: A long name is not a complete process record
paragraphs: Anaerobic fermentation describes conditions with limited or absent oxygen. It does not, on its own, tell you that another fruit was added. Fermentation also occurs in conventional wet and dry coffee processing; it is not something invented by a label with an experimental ring. The Specialty Coffee Association’s scientific explanation links microorganisms, metabolites, bean metabolism and the precursors that matter during roasting. Outcomes depend on processing conditions and the coffee itself. Read The Fermentation Effect.

This is a useful place to slow down. An elaborate process name can convey ambition while leaving basic questions unresolved. What material entered the tank? What was deliberately introduced? Which conditions were controlled, and which were simply observed? A readable label need not describe every production detail, but it should give the buyer enough information to understand the kind of intervention being discussed.

Coffeedant’s editorial recommendation is to replace a ladder of impressive terms with a set of independent questions. Oxygen conditions, added microorganisms, other ingredients and timing can be described separately. The result is easier to interpret than assuming every new word represents a higher level of quality.

sections.title: What the science can support
paragraphs: A 2025 review of coffee fermentation and sensory quality searched research through March 2025 and synthesized findings from 22 studies. Its scope illustrates that fermentation is an active research subject with multiple processing variables. It should not be reduced to a promise that a named technique improves every coffee. A literature review can summarize studied outcomes; it cannot substitute for knowing the conditions of an individual commercial lot. Read the 2025 research review.

That distinction makes an experimental label more interesting, not less. The producer’s question can be specific while the marketing becomes broad. A reader should ask whether a described result belongs to a particular coffee, a controlled experiment or a general claim. The wider the claim, the more carefully its evidence needs to be examined.

Treat flavour language similarly. A tasting note describes a perception or an intended profile; it is not automatically an ingredient declaration. A vivid descriptor and a detailed process record can coexist, but they do different jobs. One invites you to imagine the cup. The other tells you what was done to the coffee before you bought it.

sections.title: Co-inoculation is not co-fermentation with fruit
paragraphs: A March 2025 study investigated selected yeasts and lactic-acid bacteria individually and in combination during self-induced anaerobic wet coffee fermentation. Co-inoculation in that context refers to introducing a combination of microorganisms. It is not another way of saying strawberries or another fruit were added. The study is an example of a particular experimental design, not a prescription for any producer or an explanation of every coffee bearing an anaerobic label. Read the co-inoculation study.

This difference matters when asking a retailer for clarification. “It uses fermentation” does not tell the reader whether the intervention involved microorganisms, a non-coffee ingredient, or both. A useful answer names what was introduced and at what stage. The category can still be exciting without blurring the description.

For original explanatory media, show microorganisms as one input and other ingredients as another. Leave room for either input to be absent. Avoid drawing an ingredient arrow into every anaerobic tank, which would teach the wrong association. The graphic should help a reader formulate a better question, not make a disputed commercial label look more standardized than it is.

sections.title: The 2026 report puts transparency in the foreground
paragraphs: The SCA’s January 2026 report, What’s in My Coffee?, documents local terms spanning targeted wild fermentation, inoculation, supplementation, co-fermentation and flavour addition. Its Colombian research involved 30 stakeholder interviewees. An estimated 620,000 kilograms of infused, co-fermented or flavoured green coffee were produced in Colombia in 2024. This combines several styles and is an interview-based estimate, not a representative global market census. The report includes draft communication guidance, not a binding universal classification. Read the SCA primary report.

The word “draft” deserves to stay visible. It tells readers that an industry is working through a vocabulary, rather than announcing that every bag already belongs to an agreed category. A transparent seller can still describe the actual method while terminology develops. Waiting for a perfect label is not necessary to answer a straightforward question about ingredients and timing.

The market figure should be read just as carefully. It gives scale to a defined investigation in a defined place and year. It does not justify a claim that most experimental coffee uses added flavour, or that every intense fruit note has the same origin.

sections.title: A flavour impression is not an accusation
paragraphs: In September 2026, UK roaster Scenery published its position on undocumented additions and outlined a more explicit way to present coffees with added flavourings. The statement is valuable as a primary example of one business responding to the issue. It is not an independent prevalence study or evidence against unnamed competitors. Read the roaster’s September 2026 statement.

This is where a reader’s curiosity must remain distinct from suspicion. An unusual cup can motivate a question without proving misconduct. Do not turn “this tastes remarkably like fruit” into an allegation that a producer concealed an ingredient. Ask for a process explanation, then evaluate the explanation and its supporting records. If the answer is incomplete, report the incompleteness rather than inventing the missing facts.

The same principle applies to enthusiasm. A charming producer story should not resolve every uncertainty either. Readers benefit from a culture in which clear questions are welcome and honest disclosures do not require defensive language. Innovation is easier to appreciate when the buyer understands what is being offered.

sections.title: Build a process passport for the coffee you choose
paragraphs: A concise process passport can contain four entries: the starting coffee material, oxygen conditions, deliberate additions and when those additions occurred. This is Coffeedant’s proposed reader framework, not a new certification. It works because it leaves the actual method visible. The seller can supply a narrative explanation alongside the entries, and the reader can decide whether that product matches their curiosity or preference.

Begin with your own question. If you want to explore selected microorganisms, say so. If you are interested in fruit additions, ask which fruit and at which stage. If you prefer coffees without other ingredients, request that clearly. None of those preferences needs to become a verdict on every other approach. What matters is that the product description allows a meaningful choice.

The flavour frontier will remain attractive because it promises discovery. Its editorial challenge is to make discovery informed. A striking coffee can be discussed as a collaboration of raw material and method, without pretending that a tasting note reveals the whole production history. The strongest next step is a better explanation beside the vivid descriptor: enough information for the reader to enjoy the surprise and understand how it was pursued.

takeaway: Read oxygen, microorganisms, ingredients and timing separately. Welcome experimentation, ask for a clear process record, and do not treat a vivid fruit note as proof of an undisclosed addition.

faqs.q: Does anaerobic mean that fruit was added?
faqs.a: No. It describes oxygen conditions; additions require a separate explanation.

faqs.q: Can a strawberry note tell me the ingredients?
faqs.a: A descriptor is not an ingredient declaration. Ask how the coffee was processed rather than inferring a hidden ingredient.

faqs.q: Are the SCA’s 2026 recommendations a universal certification?
faqs.a: No. The cited report includes draft guidance and documents terminology still under discussion.
